name: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) high dose

lead: Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is an essential, over-the-counter vitamin. Some skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very large amounts hoping for less skin oil and fewer breakouts.

B5 is needed to make coenzyme A, which takes part in fatty acid metabolism, and proponents reason that this link could affect sebum. No clinical studies of high-dose B5 for acne or sebum were found, and the reference sources consulted do not discuss acne.

paras: It is taken as an oral supplement, usually as a standalone capsule or powder added to an existing supplement stack, for several weeks before users judge changes in skin oiliness. Some pair it with a normal cleanser and moisturizer routine.

No tolerable upper intake level has been set by US or European authorities because no harm from high intakes has been documented in humans. Some community members describe breakouts of their own while taking it; no published studies were identified on this.

web.title: Pantothenic acid-based supplement in facial acne RCT (PMC)

angle.text: Skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very high-dose vitamin B5 hoping to reduce skin oil and breakouts. The theory draws on B5's role in fatty acid metabolism; no acne trials were found.

lead: High-dose vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is the use of supplemental pantothenic acid at amounts far above the dietary requirement in the hope of clearer, less oily skin and fewer acne breakouts. Pantothenic acid is a water-soluble vitamin that animals need to make coenzyme A, which is involved in energy metabolism and fatty acid synthesis.[1] Proponents in skincare and looksmaxxing circles discuss large intakes as a way to reduce skin oil and acne lesions.

A hypothesis paper published in 1995 proposed that acne reflects a deficiency of pantothenic acid, and a 2014 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested a pantothenic acid-based supplement in 48 adults with mild to moderate facial acne.[2] Over 12 weeks, the group taking about 4.4 g per day showed a significantly larger fall in total lesion count than placebo, with fewer inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions and better quality-of-life scores.[2]

The Adequate Intake for adults in the US is 5 mg per day, and no upper intake limit has been set by US or European authorities because no human evidence of harm from high doses has been found.[1] Some commercially sold supplements contain up to 1,000 mg per capsule.[1]

paras: Deficiency is very rare in humans and has been documented mainly in prisoners of war, starvation victims and small volunteer experiments; symptoms include fatigue, irritability and numbness or burning in the extremities.[1] Roger Williams named the vitamin in 1933, and Fritz Lipmann received the 1953 Nobel Prize for discovering coenzyme A.[1]
Pantethine, a distinct compound formed from two pantothenic acid units, has been reported to lower LDL cholesterol at higher doses, whereas plain pantothenic acid does not share that effect.[1]

The acne idea traces to a 1995 paper by Leung proposing that pantothenic acid deficiency underlies acne vulgaris; the 2014 trial cites it as background but did not test the deficiency hypothesis itself.[2] The trial authors suggest antibacterial and skin-softening effects linked to coenzyme A metabolism in the epidermis and state that the exact mechanism is not understood.[2]

Topical dexpanthenol, the alcohol form that converts to pantothenic acid in the skin, is a separate use: a randomized trial found it enhanced skin barrier repair and reduced inflammation after irritation by sodium lauryl sulphate, and a review covers its use in skin disorders.[3][4]

Wikipedia's acne article notes that vitamin B12 taken above recommended intake has been reported to cause acne-like eruptions or worsen existing acne.[5] This concerns a different vitamin; the sources consulted here describe no published reports linking high-dose pantothenic acid itself to breakouts.

The main human study is a 2014 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial run at two New York dermatology sites. Of 48 randomized adults with mild to moderate acne (41 evaluable), those taking the pantothenic acid-based tablet (2.2 g per four-tablet dose, two tablets twice daily) had a significantly greater reduction in total lesion count at week 12 (P = 0.0197), a significant fall in non-inflammatory and inflammatory lesions, and lower DLQI scores (1.93 versus 5.3).[2] Investigator-rated improvement of at least one rank was 85.7 percent versus 35.7 percent.[2]

The supplement was reported as well tolerated, with two unrelated adverse events and one withdrawal because the tablets were large.[2] The authors list a short duration, small sample and sponsor ties to the product's maker among the limitations, and call for further placebo-controlled trials.[2]

timeline.event: Roger Williams names pantothenic acid after finding it in nearly every food tested.[1]
Fritz Lipmann wins the Nobel Prize for discovering coenzyme A.[1]
Leung proposes pantothenic acid deficiency as a pathogenesis of acne.[2]
Randomized placebo-controlled trial of a pantothenic acid-based supplement in facial acne published in Dermatology and Therapy.[2]
